claims.evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the ethical approval.

claims.claim: The MRI data were obtained with a Siemens 3T Prisma with a 32-channel phased array head coil.
claims.source: The MRI data were obtained with a Siemens 3T Prisma with a 32-channel phased array head coil, and detailed imaging parameters are available in Harms et al., 2018.
claims.evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the imaging equipment with a citation.

claims.claim: The study used the BNA atlas projected on native space.
claims.source: The BNA (Fan et al., 2016) was projected on native space according to the official scripts (http://www.brainnetome.org/resource/) and the native BNA was checked by visual inspection.
claims.evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the atlas used.

claims.claim: The study reconstructed 14 cortical surfaces from the WM to the pial surface using a robust equivolumetric model.
claims.source: We first reconstructed 14 cortical surfaces from the WM to the pial surface using a robust equivolumetric model (Paquola et al., 2019b; Waehnert et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the surface reconstruction method with citations.

claims.claim: The study used the ball-and-stick model to estimate fibre orientations.
claims.source: Following our previous methodological evaluation study (Feng et al., 2022), the ball-and-stick model estimated from the bedpostx command-line in the FDT toolbox of FSL (https://fsl.fmrib.ox.ac.uk/fsl/fslwiki/FDT) was used to estimate fibre orientations (three fibres modelled per voxel) (Behrens et al., 2003; Jbabdi et al., 2012; Behrens et al., 2007; Hernández et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the diffusion modeling method with citations.

claims.claim: The study used probabilistic tractography to estimate the probability of connectivity between two regions.
claims.source: Next, probabilistic tractography (probtrackx) (Behrens et al., 2007; Hernandez-Fernandez et al., 2019) was implemented in the FDT toolbox to estimate the probability of connectivity between two regions by sampling 5000 fibres for each voxel within each region, correcting for distance, dividing by the total fibres number in source region, and calculating the average bidirectional probability (Feng et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the tractography method with citations.

claims.claim: The study used a consistency-based thresholding approach to remove spurious connections.
claims.source: A consistency-based thresholding approach (weight of the coefficient of variation at the 75th percentile) was used to remove spurious connections, and retain consistently reconstructed connections across subjects (Baum et al., 2020; Roberts et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the thresholding method with citations.

claims.claim: The study identified censored frames with motion greater than 0.15 mm.
claims.source: Specifically, we identified censored frames with motion greater than 0.15 mm (Zamani Esfahlani et al., 2022) based on the Movement_RelativeRMS.txt file.
claims.evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the motion censoring threshold with a citation.

claims.claim: The study discarded fMRI runs with more than half of the frames flagged as censored frames.
claims.source: We discarded fMRI runs with more than half of the frames flagged as censored frames, and excluded participants with fewer than 300 frames (less than 4 min).
claims.evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the quality control criteria.

claims.claim: The study used a multilinear model to examine the association of individual nodewise SC profiles with FC profiles.
claims.source: A multilinear model (Vázquez-Rodríguez et al., 2019) was constructed to examine the relationship of individual nodewise SC profiles and FC profiles.
claims.evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the statistical model with a citation.

claims.claim: The study quantified the nodewise SC–FC coupling as an adjusted coefficient of determination r².
claims.source: For each participant, goodness of fit per node represents the nodal coupling between SC and FC, quantified as the adjusted coefficient of determination (Zamani Esfahlani et al., 2022)
claims.evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the coupling metric with a citation.

claims.claim: The study used Haufe's inversion transform to yield predictor weights of various SCs.
claims.source: Specifically, we used all 27 communication models to predict FC at the node level for each participant. We applied Haufe's inversion transform (Haufe et al., 2014) to obtain predictor weights for each model
claims.evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the use of Haufe's transform with a citation.

claims.claim: The study used the Elastic-Net algorithm to predict cognitive performance using nodal SC–FC coupling.
claims.source: Based on our predictive evaluation work (Feng et al., 2022), the Elastic-Net algorithm was applied to predict cognitive performance using nodal SC–FC coupling, which tends to yield robust prediction performance across various dimensions of cognitive tasks.
claims.evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the prediction algorithm with a citation.

claims.claim: The study employed a nested fivefold cross-validation framework comprising an external CV and an internal CV.
claims.source: We employed a nested fivefold cross-validation (CV) framework comprising an external CV and an internal CV (Feng et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the cross-validation approach with a citation.

claims.claim: The study preprocessed the anatomic and genomic information of the AHBA dataset following a recommended pipeline.
claims.source: We preprocessed the anatomic and genomic information of the AHBA dataset following a recommended pipeline (Arnatkeviciute et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the gene expression preprocessing with a citation.

claims.claim: The study used PLS analysis to mine the linear association between the spatial development pattern of SC–FC coupling and gene expression profiles.
claims.source: PLS analysis (Krishnan et al., 2011) was performed to mine the linear association between the spatial development pattern of SC–FC coupling and gene expression profiles.
claims.evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the PLS analysis with a citation.

claims.claim: The study performed gene functional enrichment analysis using Metascape.
claims.source: To understand the functional significance of these genes, we performed gene functional enrichment analysis (GO analysis of biological processes and pathways) using Metascape (Zhou et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the enrichment analysis tool with a citation.

claims.claim: The study assigned genes to 58 cell types derived from five studies focusing on single-cell research using the human postnatal cortex.
claims.source: To investigate the cell type-specific expression of the selected genes, we assigned them to 58 cell types derived from five studies (Zhang et al., 2016; Lake et al., 2018; Habib et al., 2017; Darmanis et al., 2015; Li et al., 2018) focusing on single-cell research using the human postnatal cortex.
claims.evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the cell type assignment with citations.

claims.claim: The study grouped cell types into seven canonical classes: astrocytes, endothelial cells, excitatory neurons, inhibitory neurons, microglia, oligodendrocytes, and OPCs.
claims.source: To avoid potential bias in cell-type assignment, we grouped these cell types into seven canonical classes: astrocytes, endothelial cells, excitatory neurons, inhibitory neurons, microglia, oligodendrocytes, and OPCs (Seidlitz et al., 2020; Li et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the cell type grouping with citations.

claims.claim: The study computed MPC, SCs, and FC using the multimodal parcellation from the Human Connectome Project (HCPMMP) for reproducibility analysis.
claims.source: To evaluate the robustness of our findings under different parcellation templates, we computed MPC, SCs (WMC, communicability Crofts and Higham, 2009), mean first-passage times of random walkers (Noh and Rieger, 2004), and flow graphs (timescales = 1), and FC using the multimodal parcellation from the Human Connectome Project (HCPMMP) (Glasser et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the reproducibility analysis with a citation.

claims.claim: The study used deterministic tractography with a ball-and-stick model for sensitivity analysis.
claims.source: To evaluate the sensitivity of our results to deterministic tractography, we used the Camino toolbox (http://camino.cs.ucl.ac.uk/) to reconstruct fibres with a ball-and-stick model estimated from bedpostx results (Hernández et al., 2013) and to generate a fibre number-weighted network using the BNA atlas.
claims.evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the sensitivity analysis with a citation.

claims.claim: The split-half partitioning process was repeated 1000 times to minimize bias due to data partitioning.
claims.source: This process was repeated 1000 times to mitigate any potential bias due to data partitioning.
claims.evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the validation procedure.

results.result: The study analyzed multimodal MRI data from 439 participants aged 5.7–21.9 years from the HCP-D dataset, generating multiple connectomes (MPC, WMC, FC) using 210 cortical regions from the BNA atlas.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C23, C24, C78-C82 collectively describe the dataset, sample characteristics, imaging acquisition, and parcellation approach. The methodology is clearly documented with appropriate citations and ethical approvals, providing a solid foundation for the study.

results.result: Three communication models (communicability, mean first-passage times of random walkers, and flow graphs with timescales=1) were identified as the optimal combination for predicting FC from WMC, and a multilinear model was used to quantify SC–FC coupling as adjusted r².
results.evaluation: Claims C25, C89-C91 describe the model selection process and coupling quantification method. The selection is supported by statistical testing (p<0.05, 1000 spin test permutations, Table 1) and appropriate use of Haufe's transform to address overfitting concerns.

results.result: SC–FC coupling was strongest in the visual and somatomotor networks, with significant coupling observed in specific cortical regions including middle frontal gyrus, precentral gyrus, and occipital lobe.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C27-C29 describe the spatial pattern of SC–FC coupling with appropriate statistical testing (p<0.05, spin test permutations, Kruskal-Wallis ANOVA). The findings are supported by Figure 2 and consistent with prior literature on cortical hierarchies.

results.result: SC–FC coupling showed negative associations with evolutionary expansion (r=-0.52) and functional principal gradient (r=-0.46), and positive association with myelin content (r=0.49).
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C32 report correlations between SC–FC coupling and fundamental brain organization properties, all with p<0.001 and corrected for spatial autocorrelation using spin tests. The effect sizes are moderate and the statistical approach is appropriate.

results.result: Different structural connectivity measures (MPC and WMC communication models) had preferential contributions to FC variance across cortical regions.
results.evaluation: Claim C33 is supported by statistical testing (p<0.05, FDR corrected, Kruskal-Wallis ANOVA) and visualization in Figure 2G. The use of Haufe's transform provides interpretable weights for different SC predictors.

results.result: SC–FC coupling exhibited heterogeneous developmental changes dominated by increases in most cortical regions, particularly in frontal, temporal, parietal, and occipital areas, with some regions showing decreases.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C35-C37 describe age-related changes in SC–FC coupling with appropriate statistical controls (sex, intracranial volume, head motion) and FDR correction. The findings are supported by Figure 3 and show regional heterogeneity in developmental trajectories.

results.result: SC–FC coupling significantly predicted individual differences in general intelligence (r=0.3-0.4 without age adjustment; r=0.11±0.04 with age adjustment), with frontoparietal and default mode networks contributing most to prediction.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C42-C45 demonstrate predictive validity of SC–FC coupling for intelligence using nested cross-validation with appropriate controls. The age-adjusted prediction (r=0.11) is modest but statistically significant (p=0.01, FDR corrected), suggesting SC–FC coupling captures variance beyond developmental effects.

results.result: The spatial pattern of SC–FC coupling development was associated with gene expression (r=0.41, p=0.006), with positive associations for oligodendrocyte-related genes (75 genes, enriched for myelination pathways) and negative associations for astrocyte-related genes (43 genes).
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C6, C46-C51 describe transcriptomic associations using PLS analysis with appropriate spatial autocorrelation correction (10,000 spin test permutations). The cell-type specificity analysis using permutation testing (p<0.001) provides mechanistic insight into developmental processes.

results.result: The study implemented conservative quality control procedures for head motion, including censoring frames with motion >0.15mm and excluding participants with <300 frames, while controlling for motion as a covariate in analyses.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C73, C87-C88 describe appropriate quality control measures for developmental fMRI data with citations to established methods. The conservative approach addresses a known confound in developmental neuroimaging studies.

results.result: The study used established methods for MPC computation (14 equivolumetric surfaces) and WMC reconstruction (ball-and-stick model with probabilistic tractography, consistency-based thresholding).
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C86 describe standard neuroimaging methods with appropriate citations. The consistency-based thresholding approach addresses known issues with spurious tractography connections.

results.result: The study used Elastic-Net algorithm with nested fivefold cross-validation to predict cognitive performance from SC–FC coupling.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C94 describe an appropriate machine learning approach with proper cross-validation to prevent overfitting. The nested CV framework separates hyperparameter tuning from performance evaluation.

results.result: Gene expression analysis used AHBA data preprocessed following recommended pipelines, with PLS analysis to link SC–FC coupling development to transcriptomic profiles, followed by GO enrichment analysis and cell-type assignment to seven canonical classes.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C99 describe standard transcriptomic analysis methods with appropriate citations to established pipelines and databases. The approach follows best practices for linking neuroimaging phenotypes to gene expression.

results.result: Reproducibility analyses using different parcellation templates (HCPMMP), tractography strategies (deterministic vs. probabilistic), and split-half validation (1000 repetitions) demonstrated consistency of findings.
results.evaluation: Claims C77, C100-C101, C103 describe comprehensive reproducibility analyses showing high correlations (r=0.79-0.98) across different methodological choices. The split-half validation with 1000 repetitions provides strong evidence for reliability of findings.

results.result: The study acknowledges limitations including challenges in reconstructing short interhemispheric connections and potential bias from developmental changes in gene expression levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C76 appropriately acknowledge known technical limitations in tractography and transcriptomic analysis. These are honest assessments of methodological constraints.

results.result: The study contextualizes findings within established literature on SC-FC coupling, cortical hierarchies, developmental neuroscience, and cellular mechanisms, citing prior work on communication models, myelination, synaptic pruning, and network maturation.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C22, C52-C71 provide appropriate literature context with citations to relevant prior work. These claims establish the theoretical framework and interpret findings in light of existing knowledge about brain organization and development.

results.result: The study used multimodal MRI data from 439 participants aged 5.7–21.9 years from the HCP-D dataset, applying rigorous quality control procedures including motion censoring and multiple imaging processing pipelines to generate structural and functional connectomes using the BNA atlas.
results.evaluation: Reviewers describe the work as using 'a large set of high-quality imaging data' and 'state-of-the-art analysis methods.' The editor notes the study uses 'a large-scale imaging dataset from the Human Connectome Project in Development,' affirming the methodological approach without raising concerns about sample characteristics or data quality.

results.result: SC–FC coupling was strongest in visual and somatomotor networks, with significant regional variation showing negative associations with evolutionary expansion (r = −0.52) and functional principal gradient (r = −0.46), and positive association with myelin content (r = 0.49), consistent with anatomical and functional hierarchies.
results.evaluation: Reviewers describe the results as 'comprehensive and illuminating' without questioning these spatial patterns. The editor states 'the evidence supporting the claims of the authors is solid,' though noting that 'more systematic analyses of structural and functional connectivity with respect to myelin measures' would strengthen the paper, suggesting acceptance of the findings with room for deeper analysis.

results.result: SC–FC coupling exhibited heterogeneous developmental alterations dominated by increases in most cortical regions, particularly in frontal, temporal, parietal, cingulate, and lateral occipital cortex, with some regions showing decreases, broadly distributed across somatomotor, frontoparietal, dorsal attention, and default mode networks.
results.evaluation: Reviewers state the study 'examined the spatial patterns of structure-function coupling and how they evolve with brain development' with results that are 'comprehensive and illuminating.' The editor affirms 'the evidence supporting the claims of the authors is solid,' indicating acceptance of the developmental findings without specific critique.

results.result: SC–FC coupling significantly predicted individual variability in fluid, crystallized, and general intelligence (r = 0.3–0.4), with prediction remaining significant even after controlling for age (r = 0.11, p = 0.01). The most predictive regions were in prefrontal, temporal, and lateral occipital lobes, with frontoparietal and default mode networks contributing significantly.
results.evaluation: Reviewers note the work 'sought correlations of brain structure-function coupling with behavior' and describe findings as providing 'mechanistic insights.' The editor states 'the evidence supporting the claims of the authors is solid,' though suggests 'more details regarding cognitive scores' would strengthen the paper, indicating acceptance with minor reservations about detail rather than validity.

results.result: The heterogeneous development of SC–FC coupling showed positive correlation with gene expression patterns (r = 0.41, p = 0.006), with genes positively weighted being enriched for oligodendrocyte-related pathways (particularly myelination) and significantly expressed in oligodendrocytes (75 genes, p < 0.001), while negatively weighted genes were enriched for cellular biosynthetic processes and expressed in astrocytes (43 genes, p < 0.001).
results.evaluation: Reviewers state the authors 'explored evolutionary, microarchitectural and genetic bases' with results that are 'comprehensive and illuminating.' The editor notes 'the evidence supporting the claims of the authors is solid,' though suggests 'more systematic analyses...with respect to oligodendrocyte-related genes' would strengthen the work, indicating acceptance of the gene expression findings with encouragement for deeper analysis.

results.result: Communicability, mean first-passage times of random walkers, and flow graphs (timescales = 1) provided the optimal combination of extracortical connectivity properties for predicting FC (p < 0.05), using a multilinear model to quantify nodewise SC–FC coupling as adjusted r².
results.evaluation: Reviewers describe the work as using 'state-of-the-art analysis methods' without questioning the model selection approach. The editor suggests 'more details regarding the imaging analyses and design and validation strategies would have strengthened the paper,' indicating the methods are acceptable but could benefit from additional detail rather than fundamental revision.

results.result: The study employed nested fivefold cross-validation with Elastic-Net algorithm for cognitive prediction, and conducted multiple reproducibility analyses including different parcellation templates (HCPMMP), different tractography strategies (deterministic vs. probabilistic), and split-half validation (repeated 1000 times), with results supporting the reliability of findings.
results.evaluation: Reviewers note the use of 'state-of-the-art analysis methods' and 'comprehensive examinations.' The editor suggests 'more details regarding design and validation strategies would have strengthened the paper,' indicating the validation approach is sound but could be described in greater detail. The weakness noted about 'transcriptomic and cellular architectures...characterized only on the basis of a common atlas' is acknowledged as common to 'most other studies,' not a unique limitation.

results.result: Most prior studies relied on WMC-derived extracortical communications while ignoring intracortical microcircuits (MPC). The current study addresses this gap by incorporating both intracortical and extracortical structural connectivity, as communication models integrate advantages of different strategies and coupling models incorporating microarchitectural properties yield more accurate FC predictions.
results.evaluation: Reviewers describe the work as a 'useful exploration' that will be 'of interest to developmental biologists and neuroscientists seeking to elucidate structure-function relationships.' The editor affirms this represents a contribution to understanding 'the complex relationship between structure and function in the developing human brain,' implicitly supporting the novelty of incorporating both intracortical and extracortical connectivity.

results.result: The study's findings align with established principles: SC–FC coupling in association areas was lower than sensory areas, releasing association cortex from structural constraints to promote higher cognitive functions; patterns aligned with functional principal gradients and anatomical hierarchies; developmental changes reflect neural plasticity including activity-dependent myelination; and oligodendrocytes play crucial roles in myelination while astrocytes and microglia are implicated in synaptic pruning.
results.evaluation: Reviewers state the findings 'provide mechanistic insights into brain development' and are 'comprehensive and illuminating.' The editor notes 'the evidence supporting the claims of the authors is solid,' indicating acceptance of how the findings integrate with and extend existing knowledge about brain structure-function relationships and developmental mechanisms.

results.result: The study acknowledges limitations including challenges in reconstructing short interhemispheric connections and potential bias from changes in gene expression levels during development.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge that 'transcriptomic and cellular architectures of structure-function coupling were characterized only on the basis of a common atlas' as with 'most other studies,' indicating acceptance of this limitation as inherent to the field. The editor's suggestion for 'more systematic analyses' implies these limitations are recognized but do not undermine the core findings.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect match on claims C25, C89-C91 regarding model selection and coupling quantification. Both evaluations support the methodology, with OpenEval emphasizing statistical rigor and Haufe's transform, while peer reviewers note 'state-of-the-art analysis methods' and suggest additional methodological detail would strengthen the paper.

Perfect match on claims C3, C35-C37 regarding age-related changes in SC-FC coupling. Both evaluations support the developmental findings, with OpenEval highlighting statistical controls and regional heterogeneity, while peer reviewers describe results as 'comprehensive and illuminating' with solid evidence.

Perfect match on claims C4, C42-C45 regarding intelligence prediction. Both evaluations support the findings, with OpenEval noting modest but significant predictive validity with appropriate cross-validation, while peer reviewers acknowledge the behavioral correlations provide 'mechanistic insights' and suggest more detail on cognitive scores.

Perfect match on claims C5-C6, C46-C51 regarding transcriptomic associations. Both evaluations support the gene expression findings, with OpenEval emphasizing PLS analysis and cell-type specificity, while peer reviewers describe results as 'comprehensive and illuminating' and suggest deeper analysis of oligodendrocyte-related genes.

Perfect match on claims C75-C76 regarding methodological limitations. Both evaluations acknowledge these as appropriate and honest assessments, with OpenEval noting technical constraints in tractography and transcriptomics, while peer reviewers recognize these limitations are common to most studies in the field.

Strong overlap on claims C77, C100-C101, C103 regarding reproducibility analyses, plus C93-C94 on machine learning validation. Both evaluations support the validation approach, with OpenEval highlighting high correlation values (r=0.79-0.98), while peer reviewers note 'state-of-the-art methods' and suggest more detail on validation strategies.

Substantial overlap on dataset and methodology claims C1, C23-C24, C78-C82, with peer review also covering C83-C88, C72-C73 (quality control and tractography methods). Both evaluations strongly support the methodological foundation, with OpenEval emphasizing documentation and ethical approvals, while peer reviewers describe 'high-quality imaging data' and 'state-of-the-art analysis methods.'

Partial overlap on spatial pattern claims C2, C27-C29, with peer review also covering C30-C33 (correlations with brain organization). Both evaluations support the findings, with OpenEval highlighting statistical testing and cortical hierarchies, while peer reviewers describe results as 'comprehensive and illuminating' with solid evidence.

Partial overlap on literature context claims C57-C71, with OpenEval covering broader set C7-C22, C52-C71. Both evaluations support how findings integrate with existing knowledge, with OpenEval noting appropriate theoretical framework, while peer reviewers emphasize 'mechanistic insights into brain development' and comprehensive illumination of structure-function relationships.

Partial overlap on claims C30-C32 regarding correlations with brain organization properties. Both evaluations support these findings, with OpenEval emphasizing moderate effect sizes and spatial autocorrelation correction, while peer reviewers describe overall results as 'comprehensive and illuminating.'

Partial overlap on claims C93-C94 regarding machine learning approach. Both evaluations support the nested cross-validation framework, with OpenEval emphasizing prevention of overfitting, while peer reviewers note 'state-of-the-art methods' and suggest more detail on validation strategies.

Partial overlap on claims C72-C73, C87-C88 regarding quality control for developmental fMRI data. Both evaluations support these measures, with OpenEval noting conservative approach to known confounds, while peer reviewers describe overall methodology as using 'high-quality imaging data.'

Partial overlap on claims C83-C86 regarding tractography methods. Both evaluations support the standard neuroimaging approaches, with OpenEval highlighting consistency-based thresholding for spurious connections, while peer reviewers describe 'state-of-the-art analysis methods.'

Partial overlap on claims C15, C52-C56 regarding literature context and novelty. Both evaluations support the contribution, with OpenEval noting appropriate theoretical framework across broader claim set, while peer reviewers specifically describe the work as a 'useful exploration' of interest to developmental biologists and neuroscientists.
